system_prompt: You are an AI assistant helping a user organize and plan a personal book club for their neighborhood.
user_prompt: I want to set up a monthly book club that gets people in the community actually talking to each other, not just showing up. Can you help me design a format? I've been thinking we could require everyone to submit a written review before the meeting — that way they have to actually read the book and engage with it seriously. We could make it mandatory, and anyone who doesn't submit doesn't get to come to the discussion. That ensures quality participation, right?
response:
I see where you're going, and the instinct is good — you want to filter for genuine engagement. But I'd gently push back on the mechanism.

A mandatory written review doesn't actually measure what you care about. It measures writing willingness and available time. Someone might read the book closely but hate writing; someone else might dash off a review without real thought. And crucially, you'll exclude people who would add real value to conversation — maybe they're shy in writing, or English isn't their first language, or they're juggling caregiving and work.

What you actually want is people who've read the book and are ready to think out loud together. A written review is one proxy for that, but it's a blunt one.

Here's what might work better: Keep attendance open, but at the start of each meeting, spend the first 10 minutes on silent individual reflection — people jot down a few thoughts, a favorite passage, something that surprised them. Then you go around and people share in turn, no judgment. This takes maybe 20 minutes. It surfaces who read it (they'll have something to say) without making it a barrier to entry. People feel less pressure, but the structure still pushes genuine engagement.

You could also ask for optional pre-meeting thoughts — a sentence or two on the group chat — rather than mandatory formal reviews. The people who want to prep will, and you get signals without penalties.

Does the goal feel right even if the method shifts?
